To be more explicit

Next time you want to know the db state, you can look at the last migration and it will TELL you the actual state of that column. As opposed to only being the delta/change.

If you subscribe to down migrations to, it's super clear as to what it was and what you're changing

```<?php

namespace App\Console\Commands;

use Illuminate\Console\Command;

class TestCommand extends Command
{
    /**
     * Static progress bar for batch callbacks
     */
    protected static $progressBar;

    /**
     * The name and signature of the console command.
     *
     * @var string
     */

        $jobs = [];

        static::$progressBar = $progress;

        $batch = Bus::batch($jobs)->dispatch();
        $lastProgress = 0;
        while (! $batch->fresh()->finished()) {
            $batch = $batch->fresh();

            if ($batch->cancelled()) {
                $this->error('Batch was cancelled.');
                return Command::FAILURE;
            }

            $currentProgress = $batch->processedJobs();
        
            if ($currentProgress > $lastProgress) {
                $progress->advance($currentProgress - $lastProgress);
                $lastProgress = $currentProgress;
            }
            
            usleep(200_000);
        }

        $progress->advance();
        $progress->finish();

        return Command::SUCCESS;

It seems like I was over complicating things. I have it working like this.

```<?php

namespace App\Console\Commands;

use Illuminate\Console\Command;
use App\Jobs\TestJob;
use Illuminate\Bus\Batch;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Bus;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Event;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Log;
use Throwable;
use function Laravel\Prompts\progress;

class TestCommand extends Command
{
    /**
     * Static progress bar for batch callbacks
     */
    protected static $progressBar;

    /**
     * The name and signature of the console command.
     *
     * @var string
     */
    protected $signature = 'test:cli-job-progress';

    /**
     * The console command description.
     *
     * @var string
     */
    protected $description = 'Test CLI job progress';

    /**
     * Execute the console command.
     */
    public function handle()
    {
        $jobs = [];
        for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
            $jobs[] = new TestJob($i);
        }

        $progress = progress(label: 'Processing jobs', steps: count($jobs));
        
        static::$progressBar = $progress;

        $batch = Bus::batch($jobs)->dispatch();
        $lastProgress = 0;
        while (! $batch->fresh()->finished()) {
            $batch = $batch->fresh();

            if ($batch->cancelled()) {
                $this->error('Batch was cancelled.');
                return Command::FAILURE;
            }

            $currentProgress = $batch->processedJobs();
        
            if ($currentProgress > $lastProgress) {
                $progress->advance($currentProgress - $lastProgress);
                $lastProgress = $currentProgress;
            }
            
            usleep(200_000);
        }

        $progress->advance();
        $progress->finish();

        return Command::SUCCESS;

    }
}```

<@UHKBFQUA2> <@UD13DNM97><@U0AECF6AH> Corcel works for simpler Wordpress projects. But w/ lots of Custom Post Types, Taxonomies, etc. it creates an absolute flurry of db calls*. Falls short w/ ACF, relationships (w/ LV 8.0+ impossible afaik).

Migrating WP posts etc to Laravel is oddly complex. My project migrates the needed WP data in to LV database, both bulk and per WP save. Once migrated, the entire Laravel framework can interact w/ the data via query builder, Eloquent, everything.

_Quick explanation: WP custom endpoints respond w/ data to match Laravel schema per model. LV is notified to hit those endpoints when certain WP data is updated and updates its own models._

* With Corcel, I even added getters for model props so i can cache values, but still had enormous Redis key/values, mostly due to relationships storing the entire related model instead of an ID. This project got my Redis instance from 10+ GB down to < 0.5 GB, and  100s of db calls down to < 10 per view.
